transcript.text: Scarcity
GENERAL ECONOMICS
GEN-ECON-01
Time: 4 minutes
Outcome: Explain scarcity and identify tradeoffs created by limited resources
Difficulty: Beginner
THE CORE IDEA

Scarcity means people, businesses, and governments have limited resources but unlimited wants. Because resources such as time, money, labor, and raw materials are limited, choices must be made. Every choice involves a tradeoff, and those tradeoffs force individuals and societies to decide how to use scarce resources. Scarcity is the basic problem that economics studies.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Resources are limited, but wants are greater than what can be produced.
A choice must be made between competing uses.
Getting more of one thing means giving up something else.
The question focuses on limits, tradeoffs, or unmet wants.
WATCH OUT
Scarcity does not mean there is almost none of a good. It means the good is limited relative to wants. Even time and money are scarce because they have alternative uses.
WORKED EXAMPLE: CHOOSING BETWEEN SCARCE USES

A student has two hours before an exam and must choose between studying economics or finishing a history paper. The student cannot fully do both. This is scarcity because time is limited, so choosing one use means giving up the other.
CHECK YOURSELF
A city has enough money to build either a new park or repair several roads, but not both this year. Why is this an example of scarcity?

transcript.text: Quantity Theory of Money
MACROECONOMICS
MACRO-23
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Apply the quantity equation, velocity, money growth, price levels, and inflation.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

The quantity equation MV = PY links the money stock and velocity to nominal output. Its growth-rate form separates growth in money and velocity from growth in real output and the price level. When velocity is stable and real output is determined by productive capacity, persistent money growth above real-output growth produces long-run inflation rather than permanently higher real output.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
The problem uses MV = PY or relates money growth to inflation.
Velocity measures how often money supports transactions during a period.
With velocity and real output fixed, more money raises the price level.
The question distinguishes a nominal price change from a lasting real-output change.
WATCH OUT
Do not assume money growth permanently raises real output. The quantity theory connects persistent money growth to inflation, especially in the long run.
WORKED EXAMPLE: MONEY GROWTH AND INFLATION

Quantity-theory graph. The vertical axis is value of money, one divided by P; the horizontal axis is money supply M. Money demand MD slopes downward and curves toward the horizontal axis. Vertical MS1 is at 2,500 and meets MD at point a, at a money value of 2. Vertical MS2 is at 5,000 and meets MD at point b, at a money value of 1. Dashed horizontal guides mark 2 and 1. MS2 is to the right of MS1 and b is below and to the right of a. The vertical axis shows the reciprocal of the price level, not velocity V.

In this clean quantity-theory case, velocity V and real output Y are fixed. Money supply doubles from 2,500 (MS1) to 5,000 (MS2). The value of money falls from 2 at a to 1 at b. Since P is its reciprocal, P rises from 1/2 = 0.50 to 1/1 = 1.00: a 100% increase. The graph shows value of money (1/P), not velocity V in MV = PY.
CHECK YOURSELF
In MV = PY, what does P represent?

transcript.text: Game Theory Foundations: Payoff Matrices, Best Responses & Nash Equilibrium
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-49
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Read payoff matrices and identify best responses, dominant strategies, and Nash equilibrium.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Game theory represents strategic choices with players, actions, and payoffs that depend on what others do. Correctly reading the matrix is the prerequisite for identifying best responses and equilibrium. Compare mutual best responses with the combined-payoff maximum. A Nash equilibrium is a cell containing mutual best responses.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Identify the players, each player's available actions, and the payoff associated with every action combination.
For each possible rival action, mark the action that gives a player the highest payoff.
A dominant strategy is best regardless of the rival's action.
A Nash equilibrium is a cell where every player's action is a best response to the others.
WATCH OUT
Do not assume equilibrium is efficient. Compare mutual best responses with the combined-payoff maximum. A Nash equilibrium is a cell containing mutual best responses.
WORKED EXAMPLE: FINDING A NASH EQUILIBRIUM

For each rival strategy, identify the action with the larger payoff. If column X is chosen, row A gives 9 rather than 3 from row B. If column Y is chosen, row A gives 2 rather than 1 from row B. Thus, A is the row player's strictly dominant strategy. For the column player, X gives 9 rather than 3 when row A is chosen, and 2 rather than 1 when row B is chosen. Thus, X is the column player's strictly dominant strategy. Because A and X are mutual best responses, (A, X) is the unique Nash equilibrium.
CHECK YOURSELF
Why must payoff order be stated?

Externalities
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-54
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Compare private and social incentives and identify the efficient quantity.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

An externality is a cost or benefit imposed on someone outside a transaction. Negative externalities make private decision makers ignore part of social cost; positive externalities make them ignore part of social benefit. Efficiency uses all marginal social costs and benefits.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Ask whether the spillover is a cost or benefit and whether it comes from production or consumption.
Negative: MSC > MPC or MPB > MSB, so the market quantity is too high.
Positive: MSB > MPB or MPC > MSC, so the market quantity is too low.
Corrective taxes, subsidies, permits, regulation, or bargaining can internalize the spillover.
WATCH OUT
Do not label every harmful outcome an externality. A spillover must affect a third party and be missing from the market price.
WORKED EXAMPLE: NEGATIVE PRODUCTION EXTERNALITY

Negative production externality in fast-fashion garments. Horizontal axis: quantity of garments in millions, with labeled ticks from 40 to 320. Vertical axis: marginal benefit and cost, with labeled dollar ticks from 3 to 24. MPB slopes downward from 21 to 9; MPC slopes upward from 3 to 15; MSC slopes upward from 9 to 21, six dollars above MPC throughout. MPB and MPC intersect at 240 million garments and 12 dollars. MPB and MSC intersect at 160 million garments and 15 dollars. Dashed guides mark both quantities and values.

Fast-fashion production creates a $6 external cost per garment, so MSC lies $6 above MPC. The market produces 240 million garments where MPB = MPC at $12. Efficiency occurs at 160 million garments where MPB = MSC at $15, eliminating 80 million units of overproduction. A $6 corrective tax aligns private and social marginal cost.
CHECK YOURSELF
If MSB lies above MPB, is the unregulated market quantity too high or too low?
